blocks.text: We know that an object moves in a circle because of centripetal force. If the magnitude of applied force falls short of required centripetal force then the object will move away from the centre of the circle. The centrifuge (Fig. 3.8-a) functions on this basic principle.

blocks.alt: A white benchtop laboratory centrifuge with its dark grey lid raised at the back. Inside, a round grey chamber holds a ring of blue-capped sample tubes. A blue control panel with a small display and three buttons is on the front.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.8(a): A laboratory centrifuge (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.8(a)).

blocks.text: Centrifuge: It is one of the most useful laboratory device. It helps to separate out denser and lighter particles from a mixture. The mixture is rotated at high speed for a specific time. In a laboratory setup, sample tubes are used where the denser particles will settle at the bottom and lighter particles will rise to the top of the sample tubes (Fig. 3.8-b).

blocks.alt: A vertical shaft carries a hub and two horizontal arms. A holder at the end of each arm grips a sample tube lying outwards, its closed rounded end pointing away from the shaft. A curved arrow round the shaft shows the rotation.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.8(b): Sample tubes of a centrifuge, whose denser particles settle at the bottom (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.8(b)).

blocks.text: The dryer of the washing machine also functions on the principle of centrifuge. The dryer consists of a long cylinder with hundreds of small holes on its wall. Wet clothes are piled up in this cylinder, which is then rotated rapidly about its axis. Water moves outward to the walls of the cylinder and thus, drained out through the holes. In this way, clothes become dry quickly.

blocks.alt: A round white spin dryer seen from slightly above, with its white lid raised at the back and a maroon rim round the opening. Inside is the perforated drum, its wall dotted with small holes, holding a few wet clothes.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.9: The dryer of a washing machine (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.9).

blocks.text: Cream separator is another practical device which is used to separate cream form the milk. In this machine, milk is whirled rapidly. Since milk is a mixture of light and heavy particles, when it is rotated, the light particles gather near the axis of rotation whereas the heavy particles will go outwards and hence, cream can easily be separated from milk.

blocks.alt: A cream separator: a wide silver bowl for milk on top, a silver separator head below it with two curved spouts pointing out to the left, a blue motor housing beside the head, and a blue cylindrical stand on three splayed legs.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.10: A cream separator (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.10).
